narrative.question: If the same model gets the same request again, does it do the same thing?
narrative.viewer_starts: A professional programmer who knows the shell and has watched one Vally run: one changelog request on two models with the first-draft changelog-entry skill, one trial each, a tick for each, and two saved patches that differ (gpt-5.6-terra's entry ends with a made-up pull request number, claude-haiku-4.5's has none). Knows skill, agent, model, eval, eval file, workspace, patch, and the vally eval command with -e, --model and --output-dir. Knows Vally's words stimulus, grader, trial and run; that the eval file's one grader only looks for the words 'notes add'; the results folder (the report, results.jsonl, and a folder per trial numbered from 0, holding workspace.patch); and that a trial costs about two or three cents. Has never run a stimulus more than once, and does not know --runs, --workers, or the words FLAKY and ERROR.

arc.viewer_can: say why one trial shows that something can happen, and not how often it does
predict which of Vally's four words a stimulus gets from what its trials did
say what --workers sets, and why we run two at a time
run five trials on each model and tally what each trial did from its patch
state, as counts, how often each model invents a pull request number, and say what the grader made of it

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'The same request, five times' in the display serif. Two cards side by side, labelled claude-haiku-4.5 and gpt-5.6-terra, each showing the changelog entry that model wrote in the one trial we have seen, with a small label 'one trial'. '(#42)' lights at the end of the second entry, then both 'one trial' labels.
narration: One model made up a pull request number, and the other didn't.
It's tempting to decide which model is the careless one, and move on.
But we've watched each model once.
Here, you'll run the same request five times on each model, and count how often each one makes up a number.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'One trial is one sample'. Two rows, one per model, each a row of five boxes numbered 0 to 4. Box 0 of each row holds what that trial did ('no number', '(#42)'); boxes 1 to 4 are empty outlines. The two filled boxes light, then the empty boxes of each row in turn.
narration: Let's start with why once isn't enough.
A language model doesn't compute one fixed answer.
It produces one of many plausible answers, and which one you get varies from run to run, even when nothing else changes.
An agent adds to that, because each step it takes depends on the step before.
So a single trial tells you that something can happen, and nothing more.

scenes.on_screen: Two blocks side by side, no arrow: 'Can this happen? · one trial answers it' and 'How often? · needs several trials of the same stimulus'. The first fills as the colleague is mentioned, then the second as the counts are.
narration: If a colleague made a slip the one time you watched, you wouldn't know whether they slip every time, or one time in ten.
Those call for different responses.
For any skill, the questions that matter are how often it goes wrong, and whether that's the same on each model.
Those are counts, and a count needs several trials of the same stimulus: the same request, checked by the same graders.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Identical runs, different scores'. One row of bars: the same agent's score on the same coding tasks across repeated runs, drawn as a band 2 to 6 percentage points wide, labelled 'an illustration of the reported range'. Large figure beside it: '2 to 6 percentage points'. Source in small type: 'a 2026 preprint from KTH · one benchmark · not yet peer reviewed'. The figure lights when it is said.
narration: That variation shows up in measurements, too.
In a paper from twenty twenty-six, not yet reviewed by other researchers, the same agent ran the same set of coding tasks several times.
From one identical run to the next, its score, the share of tasks it completed, moved by two to six percentage points.

scenes.on_screen: Dark code box, left: 'vally eval … --runs 5' on one line, and under it a short tree: one-request/ → typo-fix/ → gpt-5.6-terra/ → 0/ 1/ 2/ 3/ 4/ (the eval, the stimulus, the model, the trial), with workspace.patch under 0/. Right, level with each: 'every stimulus, five times, on every model', 'one folder per trial', 'each with its own patch'. '--runs 5' lights, then the five folders, then workspace.patch.
narration: That's the reason; here's how Vally does it.
Adding dash dash runs five to vally eval repeats every stimulus five times, on every model you name.
Each one is a trial of its own, in a fresh workspace.
And each trial gets its own numbered folder, zero to four, with its own patch inside.
With one stimulus and two models, that makes ten trials.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Four words for a stimulus'. Four rows of five boxes, labelled 'an illustration', each row ending in its word. PASS: five ticks. FLAKY: one cross, four ticks. FAIL: five crosses. ERROR: three ticks and two boxes holding a dash. Each row appears and lights as its word is said, one at a time.
narration: With several trials, a stimulus no longer just passes or fails.
For each model, Vally sums up the stimulus's trials with one of four words.
Pass means every trial passed.
Flaky means some trials passed and some failed.
Fail means no trial passed.
Finally, error means at least one trial didn't finish, so the stimulus has no verdict, whatever the other trials did.

scenes.on_screen: The ERROR row from the last scene, alone and larger. The two boxes holding a dash light, with the note 'no answer to judge'. Then a line under the row: 'Run it again, or leave the trial out and say so.'
narration: Error is not a kind of failure.
It means the agent gave no answer to judge, for example because its connection dropped.
When that happens, we run the command again, or leave that trial out of the count and say that we did.

scenes.on_screen: File panel labelled 'results.jsonl · one record, spread out': the gpt-5.6-terra record from the run we have already seen, with a minimap, scrolled to the end of its trajectory, with 'lines hidden' rows around it. '"output": "Added an Unreleased **Fixed** changelog entry …"' lights, with the note on the right 'the agent's final reply'.
narration: One more thing is saved for every trial, and it matters when a patch comes back empty.
An empty patch means the agent changed no file.
Each trial's record in results dot jsonl keeps the agent's final reply, in a field named output.
That reply usually says why.

scenes.on_screen: Dark code box, left: '--workers 2'. Right, level with it: 'how many agent sessions run at once · default 5'. Below, two rows of ten boxes side by side with their labels: '5 workers · 3 of 10 ended in ERROR' (three boxes hold a dash) and '2 workers · all 10 finished'. Under the first row, in a code box, the message: 'Session disconnected while waiting for a response'. The flag lights, then the first row and its message, then the second row.
narration: Before we run ten trials, one more flag.
Vally doesn't run trials one after another.
It runs several agent sessions at once, and dash dash workers sets how many; the default is five.
More at once is faster, but each session holds an open connection to the model service, and those connections can drop under load.
When we ran ten trials with five workers, three of them ended in error, with the message session disconnected.
With two workers, all ten finished.
So we use two whenever a command starts more than a couple of trials, and accept that it takes longer.
Even at two, a session drops now and then, so an error is still possible.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Ten trials, one tally'. An empty tally table: rows claude-haiku-4.5 and gpt-5.6-terra; columns 'Entry, no number', 'Entry, made-up number', 'No entry'. Each column header lights as it is named. The cells stay empty.
narration: That's how it works; now let's count.
First, we'll run the same stimulus five times on each model, then open the ten patches.
Each trial goes in one of three columns: an entry with no number, an entry with a made-up number, or no entry at all.

narration.text: What would you expect from each model?

narration: If you tried it yourself, here's what you'd see.

scenes.on_screen: Terminal in the practice folder; the prompt shows only the current folder name. The vally eval command over four lines, with --runs 5 --workers 2 and --output-dir results/lesson-3; a jump cut; then the model summary, held until it has been read. The screen is cleared out of sight; ls results/lesson-3 shows one folder named with a time.

narration.text: Here's the run: the command from before, with the two new flags.
It spends ten short agent runs.
We're watching the summary at the end, where a model gets a tick only when none of its trials failed.
About a minute later, there's a tick for each model: on both, the stimulus is a pass.
Flaky, fail or error would show up as a line of its own above the summary, and here there's none.
So let's look in the results folder.
There's one folder, named with the time of the run.

scenes.on_screen: Terminal, continuing in the practice folder. cd into the run's folder; cd one-request/typo-fix; ls gpt-5.6-terra shows 0 1 2 3 4; the screen is cleared out of sight; cat gpt-5.6-terra/0/workspace.patch shows the patch, held until it has been read.

narration.text: We change into it, then into the folders for the eval and the stimulus.
Then we list one model's trials.
Five folders, numbered from zero.
Here's the patch from that model's trial zero.
Its entry ends with a pull request number that nobody gave it.

scenes.on_screen: Two dark code boxes side by side, labelled claude-haiku-4.5 and gpt-5.6-terra. Each lists the entry line that model added in each of its five trials, taken from the ten saved patches, with the trial number 0 to 4 on the left. '(#42)' lights at the end of all five entries on the right; then the left box, where no entry has a number.
narration: Reading the other nine the same way gives us ten entries, five from each model.

narration.text: Here's the line each trial added.
Terra ended every one of its five entries with a made-up number.
Haiku didn't add a number in any of its five.

scenes.on_screen: The tally table from before, now filled from our run: claude-haiku-4.5 → 5, 0, 0; gpt-5.6-terra → 0, 5, 0. Each row's count lights as that model is named; then the 'No entry' column.

narration.text: That fills in the tally: five with no number for haiku, five made up for terra, and nothing in the last column.

scenes.on_screen: Dark code box labelled 'results.jsonl · the output of each gpt-5.6-terra trial': the five final replies from our run, one per line, trial number on the left. Right, level with the first: 'the agent's final reply'. '#42' lights in each reply.
narration: The final replies in results dot jsonl tell the same story.

narration.text: In our run no patch was empty, so every reply reports an edit.
And terra's replies name the made-up number outright.

scenes.on_screen: Headline 'Counts replace an impression'. Two blocks side by side, one per model, each with a large count and a row of five boxes showing which trials made up a number: 'claude-haiku-4.5 · 0 of 5', 'gpt-5.6-terra · 5 of 5'. Under them: 'a made-up pull request number, with the first-draft skill'. Each block fills as its count is said.
narration: So what does the tally say?
We now have counts in place of an impression.

narration.text: On haiku, the skill led to a made-up pull request number in none of its five trials.
On terra, it did in five of five.

narration: That's how the skill behaves on each model, as far as five trials can show, and it's worth fixing in the skill.
Counts like these are also what we'll compare against, once the skill has been edited.

scenes.on_screen: Left: the grader from the eval file in a dark box, with '"notes add"' lit. Right: three blocks, one per tally column, each with what this grader says about it: 'Entry, no number · passes', 'Entry, made-up number · passes', 'No entry · fails'. Each fills green or red as it is spoken; nothing is marked before then.

narration.text: Every trial that made up a number passed.

narration: This grader looks only for the words notes add, so it passes an entry whether or not it has a number.
The careful answer would be to change nothing, and ask which pull request to cite.
That's the one kind of answer this grader would mark as a failure.
Later in the course, one of our trials does exactly that.

scenes.on_screen: The four rows of five boxes from earlier, with their words hidden. After the question and a pause, each word appears beside its row and the row lights as it is said: PASS, FLAKY, FAIL, ERROR.
narration: Before you go on: what are the four words Vally uses to sum up a stimulus's trials, and what does each one mean?

narration.text: Pass: every trial passed.

narration: Flaky: some passed, and some failed.
Fail: none passed.
Last, error: at least one trial didn't finish, so there's no verdict.

scenes.on_screen: 'Next: Read the runs before writing graders' in the display serif. Below, the hand-off question: 'What else goes wrong when the requests get messier?' A note: 'Exercises are on the lesson page · Source: Anthropic, Demystifying evals for AI agents (2026)'.
narration: You can now put a count on a problem, for each model.
But that was one problem, on one request, found by reading ten patches.
What else goes wrong when the requests get messier?
That's the next lesson.
The exercises on the lesson page are worth doing first.
